title: When the Harvest Burns
premise: Orsen Halloran, a pest controller in the dying farm town of Hollow Creek, is called to their late grandmother's house where every photograph now shows an extra chair at the kitchen table. The chair belongs to a founder of the town, one of six who sealed something beneath the old well with a bargain renewed each harvest—and Orsen's family has been quietly paying its debt for generations. As neighbors begin appearing in photographs who were never there at all, and the well begins to refill ahead of schedule, Orsen must uncover which founder's line they truly descend from and complete the interrupted ritual before the thing beneath remembers their name. In the end, Orsen finishes the ritual by taking the founders' seat themselves, binding the entity but erasing themselves from every photograph and memory except one: the extra chair, now permanently theirs.
about_author: Vesper Vasquez grew up in rural farm country where abandoned homesteads outnumbered streetlights, and spent years collecting local legends about wells, harvests, and things that wait. Their fiction blends folk horror with intimate family secrets, exploring how small towns survive by agreeing not to look too closely.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Called to clear 'rodents' from grandma's vacant house, Orsen finds no droppings—only that every family photograph now includes an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before. The emotional beat is quiet dread: twelve years of rational explanations begin to crack as Orsen recognizes the chair's carvings match a birthmark on their own wrist.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Researching town archives, Orsen learns of six founders who sealed something beneath the dry well in 1847, renewing a bargain each harvest. The librarian, Maren, warns them to stop asking questions. The beat is mounting unease: Orsen realizes grandma died on the exact night the chair first appeared.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Were Never Born
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Photographs across town begin showing people who don't exist—a farmer, a schoolteacher, a woman holding a child. When Orsen confronts Maren, she admits the founders' descendants have always maintained the ritual, and her own family was one of them. The beat is betrayal: loyalty to Hollow Creek means complicity.

chapters.title: Grandma's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Hidden in the house's floorboards, Orsen finds grandma's ledger recording payments made to the well for sixty years—names crossed out as debts came due, including Orsen's parents. The final entry names Orsen, dated next month. The beat is grief curdling into anger at being raised inside a lie.

chapters.title: The Refill
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. The dry well begins filling with black water weeks early, and livestock start standing motionless around it at night, facing inward. Mayor Aldous Crane publicly dismisses it while privately pressuring Orsen to leave town. The beat is isolation: staying invisible was never an option—the well chose them long ago.

chapters.title: Six Chairs
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. In the founders' meetinghouse, Orsen finds six chairs matching the phantom one and a partial ritual text; the seventh step was deliberately destroyed by whichever founder tried to break the bargain. Crane arrives and reveals he is a founder's heir—and that breaking the ritual would free what's below. The beat is vertigo: truth and loyalty point opposite directions.

chapters.title: Harvest Night
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. On the night the whole town gathers for the harvest festival, the water rises into the streets and the erased people from the photographs walk among the crowd, unrecognized. Orsen attempts the ritual alone as Crane sabotages the circle, choosing the town's comfortable lie over the truth. The beat is despair at the edge of drowning.

chapters.title: Beneath the Waterline
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Pulled under, Orsen faces the entity wearing the faces of their erased ancestors and understands the bargain: it doesn't take lives, it takes recognition—it eats being remembered. Grandma's voice guides them to the missing seventh step, hidden in the ledger's binding. The beat is terrible clarity: identity itself is the currency.

chapters.title: The Seventh Step
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Surfacing during the flood's peak, Orsen completes the ritual by claiming the founders' seat willingly—not as sacrifice imposed, but chosen. Crane drowns in the collapsing well-house, still insisting nothing is wrong. The beat is resolve: power corrupts only when hoarded, and Orsen refuses to hoard it.

chapters.title: Chair at the Table
chapters.summary: POV Orsen, then shifting to Maren in the coda. The waters recede; the town forgets the flood, the founders, and Orsen entirely. Only Maren, keeper of records, finds one photograph: an extra chair at grandma's table, warm as if just vacated. The beat is bittersweet resolution—Orsen traded memory for the town's survival, present only as the chair that waits.
